description: BioHacking Village talks from DEF CON 34.

talks.title: AIRGAP BREACHED - Monitoring Ancestral Payload from the Poles
talks.teaser: Presents a low-cost, open-source eDNA air sampler for catching ancient and airborne DNA as part of climate-linked biosurveillance.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the claim that thawing Arctic permafrost releases ancient microbes and DNA fragments into the air, creating an input stream that almost no one monitors. The speakers trace the route these fragments take: from bubbles at meltwater surfaces and wind-lifted debris, through UV exposure that shells or biofilms can partly resist, to cloud nucleation and a return to the ground in precipitation.

Next comes the hardware. The sampler is a 3D-printed housing with a small fan, a coarse pre-filter, a venturi throat that speeds airflow toward a fine membrane, and a silica desiccant chamber. A microcontroller board reads pressure, CO2-equivalent, humidity, temperature and light sensors. The build cost is put near $69, and the presenters explain that a stronger fan would add turbulence that throws DNA onto the walls. They then outline lab steps: filter removal, lysis, PCR amplification of 16S rDNA, gel checks, sequencing, and taxonomic assignment against reference databases.

The closing argument is that cheap parts and desktop printing move environmental sampling beyond well-funded institutions, and a distributed set of nodes could serve as an early-warning layer. The presenters point to open materials on GitHub and acknowledge that eDNA monitoring standards do not exist yet. For practitioners, the useful takeaways are the sampler design and the workflow outline. The talk does not present field results or validated detection performance.

talks.title: Four Newbies Vs - An Insulin Pump - How Hard Can It Be
talks.teaser: Follows four security students as they analyze a Bluetooth Low Energy insulin pump, from threat modeling to spoofing the pump's advertisements to reach the controller.
talks.summary:
Four cybersecurity students from a Norwegian university describe their bachelor thesis on a commercial tubeless insulin pump, approaching it as newcomers to medical device research. They explain how type 1 diabetes depends on insulin delivery, and how the pump pairs over Bluetooth Low Energy with a controller app that was only offered in a single region, which made even getting a compatible phone a hurdle.

The team built a threat model using STRIDE and MITRE's embedded-device framework, splitting the system into controller, pump and glucose sensor and rating each threat by impact and attack complexity. Passive captures of pairing traffic revealed vendor identifiers and a service UUID in advertisements. Scan floods and connection-request floods were blunted by rate limits and fixed pauses, but an ESP32 imitating the pump's advertisement structure eventually got the controller to open a connection. Analysis of the later key exchange pointed to elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman with no authentication of the peer.

In a demo, the controller refused to connect once it saw more than one pump, so a spoofed advertisement caused a denial of service. The speakers note that this behavior was likely added to prevent rogue connections seen in earlier pumps, and they suggest verifying the peer during connection as a fix. They stress that real-world risk is low. Their closing takeaway: a beginner's questions and persistence drove the work, and anything passively observable may be spoofable.

talks.title: Counting the Dead in the Digital Siege Detection Mapping Patient Harm
talks.teaser: Maps how ransomware attacks on hospitals translate into patient deaths, and how existing coding, certification and legal systems could be adapted to count that harm.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with evidence that ransomware attacks on hospitals raise in-hospital deaths. A Medicare-claims study cited by the speakers estimates a relative increase of 34 to 38 percent for patients already admitted when an attack begins, with the strongest effects among people with several comorbidities. Because that count covers only Medicare patients, the speakers treat the reported death toll as a floor. Regional spillover shows up as ambulance diversion, longer waits and patients leaving without being seen.

The central argument is that no current system records this harm. Breach reporting tracks data loss rather than patients. The classification systems offer device-security descriptors but no external-cause code for a cyber attack, death certificates have no field for one, and the disaster-risk hazard profiles name cyber threats without mentioning patient harm or death. The speakers propose an external-cause category, a certifier prompt and clinician documentation, all submittable through existing public revision processes instead of new treaties. A German investigation into a patient death after diversion, and a settled Alabama lawsuit, show how hard causation is to establish.

The legal segment frames the gap as a state duty. Under the right to life, states must exercise due diligence to prevent avoidable deaths and to document risks and losses, which the speakers argue places cyber attacks alongside natural disasters. They describe attribution as a chain in which technical detection comes first and the legal step is the weakest link. The closing remarks point to insurance, foreseeability in court and board oversight as levers that better data could move.

talks.title: DarkSyringe - Automated poisoning of Clinical AI Assistants Through PDFs a physician's POV
talks.teaser: Shows how plausible false medical statements hidden in PDF discharge letters can steer LLM summaries toward harmful treatment advice.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a hand surgeon, starts from the pressure on clinicians: long hours, paperwork, and growing patient workloads push doctors toward AI tools that summarize notes and answer clinical questions from uploaded documents. Their argument is that a PDF is an unvalidated input, and that classic prompt injection fails here because blunt commands conflict with the document and get flagged. The alternative they describe, divergent prompt injection, is a false but clinically plausible sentence, such as a wrong drug or an invented contraindication, that fits the surrounding text.

The talk presents DarkSyringe, an open-source pipeline that finds text-based PDFs, removes personal identifiers, asks a local model to write a harmful but believable payload, hides it in the document body with transparent text, and uses a second model to check whether the resulting summary differs in a dangerous way. In a live demo on a boxer's fracture letter, a commercial model summarized the poisoned file and recommended an unindicated antibiotic at a toxic dose, plus an invented cardiac contraindication. Tests between August and December 2025 found several frontier models vulnerable, while later detectors caught some variants and not others.

The speaker closes with defenses that help but do not solve the problem: scanning for hidden content, or rendering pages to images and running OCR. The main takeaways are that clinicians need to read sources skeptically, and that anyone building clinical tools should treat every ingested document as untrusted input.

talks.title: Human in the Loop or Human Out of Luck
talks.teaser: Shows how a rare-disease patient's involvement changed what AI-assisted student teams investigated in a Stanford course built on multi-omic data.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a patient living with complex rare conditions, describes a Stanford GENE240 course in which interdisciplinary student teams used AI-assisted tools and multi-omic data, including whole-genome sequencing and proteomics, to investigate her case. The students did not receive her electronic health records, because she worried that decades of misdiagnoses would mislead the analysis. She also arranged individual consent agreements with each student after finding the institutional consent model inadequate.

The teams reached different hypotheses from the same starting data, shaped by their choice of tools, prompts, pipelines and disciplinary instincts. One team fed everything into an AI system and received an impressive first report, but over later iterations a finding it had flagged as important disappeared from the analysis, and the recommended prescriptions vanished with it. Students could go back to the patient with questions and ask for more diagnostics, and they said this contact mattered more than working with the synthetic patients common in similar exercises.

The speaker calls the experiment valid because it narrowed and eliminated possibilities rather than producing final answers. Her case remains unresolved, and clinical translation work with her physician is still ahead. The takeaway is that patients should stay inside the interpretive loop, and that data agency, including getting one's own data back from genomic programs, matters for participatory medicine.

talks.title: Hacking Hearts by Reverse Engineering Pacemaker Firmware
talks.teaser: Follows a pacemaker patient and two students as they reverse engineer a clinic programmer and an implant's firmware, exposing its weaknesses.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with Marie Mo, a researcher who depends on a pacemaker herself. She began studying her Biotronik device in 2015, after finding no published security research on it. A radiation-induced fail-safe event, and the memory dump the clinic programmer produced during recovery, later became a lead for the wider project, which has since produced several CVEs, papers and student theses.

The student speakers walk through the ecosystem: a Windows XP programmer, a programming head acting as a radio transceiver, and the implant. From the programmer they traced the DLLs behind its dump routine and patched hard-coded address ranges, reaching the device's full 16 MB space instead of a small default region. Mapping COM vtables to interface names and hooking serial APIs let them rebuild the packet protocol in a custom tool. Firmware analysis then revealed read, write and an indirect-call command, giving arbitrary read and write. One shellcode overwrite crashed the device and had to be recovered with a reset command.

The weaknesses they list include a von Neumann layout without execute-versus-write separation, no address randomization, and no real authentication, since the device returns its connection identifier to any requester. Attacks needed close range, and the team reported the findings to the vendor, which is working on fixes. The takeaway is that obscurity does not protect implanted devices, though the speakers stress that the benefits still outweigh the risk.

talks.title: Safe, Secure, and Effective - What Static Behavior Analysis Reveals About Your Med Devices
talks.teaser: Shows how automated reverse engineering of medical device firmware maps each function to a clinical subsystem, so changes can be judged by patient safety rather than only by vulnerability.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that medical device security is often framed around vulnerabilities and CVSS scores, when the more useful question is whether a device's software behaves safely and effectively for its clinical purpose. The speaker proposes a "software bill of behaviors": a machine-readable record of what each function in a compiled binary does. The approach comes from research done under ARPA-H, and the work is being carried into the CycloneDX SBOM standard.

The method starts by decompiling firmware. In the example, about 40,000 functions were analyzed and labeled by behavior, such as reading ECG data, sending data over the network, or writing hardware configuration. Those functions were then clustered into clinical subsystems. Public FDA 510(k) summaries were used as reference for what a patient monitor should do. The case study was the Contec CMS8000 patient monitor, with 62 extracted files. It showed 35 wireless functions that were never cleared by the FDA, a hardcoded external address that received patient information, and an NFS-based path that copied and ran remote files. ECG configuration functions were reachable only through the user interface, so they were not a direct remote risk, but any change to them would matter for safety.

The speaker then compared a vendor patch against the original firmware. Only a small share of functions changed, and none of the cyber-relevant behaviors did. The original backdoor remained because it was documented design and removing it could hurt patient care, so compensating controls were needed. One patched listener's call graph changed heavily and required deeper functional checks. The practical takeaway is to classify changes by clinical impact, keep behavior records in a standard format, and check them against the threat model.

talks.title: Snap, Crackle, Popped - How to manage a massive cyber attack
talks.teaser: Panelists from a medical device maker, a hospital and the FDA walk through the first hours and days of a major healthcare cyber incident.
talks.summary:
This BioHacking Village panel brings together a former CISO of a medical device maker, the CISO of a Boston hospital, and a division director from the FDA's medical device cybersecurity group. They open with the first 45 minutes after an attack is discovered, describing how the shock of the event gives way to playbooks while teams try to judge whether they face a worst case or something manageable.

The middle of the discussion covers containment and coordination. The hospital perspective is that isolating connections is increasingly the first move, with decisions made quickly and documented so systems can be reconnected later. The regulator's focus is patient access: whether a manufacturer can keep supplying devices, whether cloud-connected products can stay online, and whether a shortage is forming. The panel also points to breakdowns between IT, emergency management and clinical teams, and to competing priorities such as clinical uptime, forensic preservation and reporting duties.

Looking toward the 72-hour mark, the speakers stress staff fatigue, rotating shifts and basic needs like rest and food as sources of error. They close on the legal balance of public communication, arguing that explaining what others can do to protect themselves matters more than assigning blame. Practitioners should take away the need to settle decision-making authority before an incident, document choices as they happen, and rehearse downtime processes.

talks.title: Wand Protocol - Full Chain Attack on an FDA Listed Fertility Analyzer
talks.teaser: Shows how an FDA-listed at-home fertility hormone analyzer can be taken over over Bluetooth, and how its app and cloud expose reproductive health records.
talks.summary:
The Northeastern University researchers examine a consumer fertility hormone analyzer that is FDA listed and used at home to track LH, FSH, estrogen and progesterone. They argue that these readings guide real decisions, such as IVF timing, so forged or leaked numbers carry physical and legal consequences. They map the data path across Bluetooth Low Energy, the companion phone app and the vendor cloud, noting that results pass through three trust boundaries where they could be altered.

The team reported about 20 separate weaknesses across those layers. The headline problem is a rogue peripheral attack. The app matches the device by a substring of its advertised Bluetooth name, so an attacker advertising a matching name receives the user's session token during the normal handshake. In a live demo, they spoofed the analyzer, got the app to connect to a laptop, and injected fake results. Other findings included a login endpoint that issued sessions without checking passwords, a hardcoded API key in the app that allowed reads and writes across many profiles, firmware reachable through an unauthenticated storage bucket, and health data sent to third-party analytics on every session open. All testing used researcher-owned hardware and accounts.

The proposed fixes are encrypted BLE with authenticated pairing, mutual authentication between app and device, integrity protection on health payloads, removal of embedded secrets, minimizing third-party telemetry, and a published disclosure policy with a software bill of materials. The vendor said it had shipped device and app updates after two patch cycles. For practitioners, the lesson is that connected medical devices need authenticated links, server-side object authorization and scrutiny of bundled tracker SDKs.

talks.title: To Catch a Pseudoscientist
talks.teaser: Explains how AI-generated papers, scam journals and gatekeeping networks push fabricated science into the public record, and offers red flags for spotting it.
talks.summary:
Dr. James Utley opens with a problem he calls the AI slop factory: publish-or-perish pressure pushes researchers to lean on generative tools at every stage, from the initial idea and literature review to grant summaries, experiment planning and data analysis. He argues that fabricated or manipulated statistics can slip through to publication, especially in scam journals that accept papers for a fee, and that the output can later feed training datasets and contaminate future model answers. The stakes, in his framing, reach patients, including clinical labs where validation can be rushed.

The middle of the talk turns to how fraud shows up in practice. He describes informal networks where the same researchers appear across many papers, and a senior co-author effect that helps weak work get accepted. The audience then brainstorms countermeasures: transparent data with third-party verification, mandatory disclosure of how AI was used, a bounty program for finding flawed research, and public accountability tied to researcher identifiers.

The closing section offers a practical checklist for reviewing a paper. Check the publication year, look for broken references such as bad DOIs or mismatched names, compare charts against tables for sample sizes, odds ratios and p-values, and treat suspicious 2023 to 2024 work with extra scrutiny. He stresses awareness over a complete fix and mentions a free biopunk book.
